rv.q: The gloriously gory, sleek, over-the-top musical that opened Thursday at the Theatre is a darkly wonderful adaptation of the once-controversial novel by Bret Easton Ellis.

Director Rupert Goold, composer Duncan Sheik and book writer Roberta Aguirre-Sacasa crank up the satirical volume on Bret Easton Ellis' cult novel in a musical with design to die for and a cool, period-appropriate electro-pop score...
A comic 'American Psycho' you can dance to? Somehow, it works.
The emptiness at the heart of “American Psycho” is the source of both its originality and its eventual tediousness.
Under the masterfully precise direction of Rupert Goold, this roller-coaster ride for the stage will have you peering over your shoulder at the well-dressed patrons behind you.
Nevertheless, the second act is disappointing.
American Psycho is a slick, well-crafted musical that succeeds in translating Bret Easton Ellis's controversial novel to the stage, even if it doesn't quite capture the book's savage bite.

Instead we get a portrait of blondes, Realtors, traders and the Hamptons that we've seen before, as played by an underused Alice Ripley and Helene Yorke, among others cavorting on Es Devlin's digitized playground.
The sum of these effects is to create a celebration of vapidity and inhumanity that is itself vapid and inhuman.

Of course, it could be argued that the “American Psycho” team has done its job too well, since you’re also likely to identify with Patrick when, shortly before he crucifies a young woman with a nail gun, he concludes solemnly that there’s “not one clear, identifiable emotion within me.”
“American Psycho” is slick, sleek and empty, a one-joke show that drowns its message, such as it is, in red sauce and fake emotion.
Still, the result is oddly evanescent, so sleek and gym-toned that any real stab at meaning or consequence slides off and away.
If the satire were more stinging, the show might stand a chance.
If only the creators of this ultimate "why" musical had paid any attention to the possibilities of that kind of subtlety, they might have come up with a bearable if not a justifiable evening.

Or to put it another way: What might have sounded on paper like an ill-advised stunt — "Let's make a show about a man losing his bearings and slaughtering dozens of people!" — ends up being the timeliest, most trenchant show of the season.
If you can resign yourself to the story’s innate ambiguity, you’re in for a perversely enjoyable experience.
As a result, the final on-stage American Psycho minutes do nothing to sustain a venture that has already overstayed its welcome.
Depending on how you look at “American Psycho,” it’s either horrifying or a hoot that audiences applaud when a musical number ends in mayhem.
The pace and interest slacken in the second act, when Bateman goes on a killing tear.
Notwithstanding all this, the piece has serious structural problems.
American Psycho is well executed – entertaining even – but what exactly is the idea?
The musical version of American Psycho is slick and stylish, with a strong performance by Benjamin Walker as Patrick Bateman, but it feels emotionally hollow.
It takes some artful dodging to bring an audience to feel any connection with the anti-hero of the piece, Patrick Bateman (Benjamin Walker).
But, lacking the shock power of the book, it's hard to see the reason for the musical.
The musical adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis' notorious novel about a homicidal yuppie is slick and stylish, but it's also emotionally hollow
This may be why “American Psycho” failed to stir me: The notion that evil lurks where we may not expect to find it isn’t shocking anymore.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this stylish but hollow musical adaptation, praising Benjamin Walker's performance and sleek 80s aesthetic while questioning whether the material works as a Broadway show.

sg.ra: Shubert/SeatPlan place rows C-E as 'just right' — close enough to catch facial detail without the stage-height skew that rows AA/A suffer inside this shallow 26'9" proscenium house; TickPick singles out row B (seats 105-110) as the best seat in the Schoenfeld.

SeatPlan notes the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but only begins clipping the top of the stage at row Q — so K-P sits in the narrow band that's still unobstructed yet priced below premium; TickPick and Headout independently flag K-P as the value pocket in this 1,079-seat Shubert house.

sg.vl: Overhang cuts the top of the stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly says rows beyond Q lose the top of the stage to the mezzanine overhang, and Headout/TickPick corroborate that under-overhang seats 'might have obstructed views from the overhang of the box seats or the mezzanine itself' — a real issue in this shallow Shubert house where the mezz projects forward.

sg.vl: Overhead sweep of the whole stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both cite front center mezz rows A-B as offering 'excellent overhead views perfect for appreciating the stage in one sweep' — the Schoenfeld's mezz hangs closer to the stage than larger Shubert houses, so row A feels surprisingly close rather than distant.

SeatPlan flags E-G as benefiting from 'great rake for aerial views which cover the entire stage below' — the Schoenfeld mezz is steeper than most Shubert houses, so E-G keeps the full stage visible where a flatter rake would start clipping; Headout calls it a value tier below the premium A-D band.

Multiple sources describe rear mezz past row F as 'a gamble... actors start to look like LEGO figures' — despite the Schoenfeld only having 392 mezz seats, the steep rake trades sightline for proximity and you lose emotional read on faces; a J104 reviewer conceded 'nearly center, no obstructions' but 2nd-to-last row.

SeatPlan notes 'single-digit seats in rows A-D' of the side mezz 'are more directly above the stage and feel surprisingly close' — the Schoenfeld's narrow 40-foot proscenium means side-mezz angles are less punishing than wider houses, though TickPick warns the far edges of rows 'have slightly blocked views of the corners of the stage'.
